title: 2. Prediction, Keywords, and Paraphrase Recognition
blocks: The engine of Listening: predicting the shape of each gap, choosing anchor keywords the exam cannot disguise, and pre-loading likely paraphrases before the audio plays.

These three skills are the engine of Listening. Prediction tells your ear what to wait for. Keywords tell your eyes where to wait. Paraphrase recognition tells you what the answer will sound like when it arrives, because it will almost never arrive in the words you expect. Master these three and half of the Listening test is already won before the audio starts.

Prediction is the habit that most separates a Band 8 candidate from a Band 6 one, and almost nobody teaches it properly. The beginner reads a question and waits. The expert reads a question and knows what is coming.

Ask, of every single gap before the audio begins: “What kind of answer am I about to hear?” That question sets a filter in your mind, and that filter is what lets you catch one word out of a flood of two hundred.

Predict on two layers. Layer 1 is the grammatical shape: is the missing word a noun, verb, adjective, or number? You can nearly always tell from the words around the gap (“open until ____” needs a time; “must not ____ inside” needs a verb; “surprisingly ____” needs an adjective; “bring your own ____” needs a countable noun). Layer 2 is the information type: name, place, measurement, date, price, object, role.
Often spelled out; listen letter by letter
A concrete noun; check singular or plural
What someone does, must do, or must avoid
A describing word about quality or attitude

Read around the gap, not just up to it. Beginners read only the words before a gap; experts read the words after it too, because the word after the gap often fixes the grammar and narrows the meaning far more than the word before. “The museum's ____ collection attracts thousands of visitors” only becomes predictable once you read past the gap to “collection,” which tells you the answer is an adjective or noun describing a type of collection.

Predict singular or plural too, since the words around a gap often reveal it (“there is a ____” forces singular; “guests are given two ____” forces plural; “each room has its own ____” forces singular). This is not only about catching the answer; a mismatch between what you predicted and what you caught is a useful alarm that you misheard.

Respect the word limit before you write. Every completion task has an instruction such as “Write ONE WORD ONLY” or “NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER.” Writing three words where two are allowed makes the answer wrong even if the meaning is perfect. Predict the length too, and do not cram in extra describing words the speaker uses if the limit is one word.

A hyphenated word (part-time, twenty-five, check-in) counts as one word. Numbers written as figures (25, 1990) count as a number, not a word. Knowing this frees you to write “part-time” under a one-word limit without fear.

Worked example: a note-completion set asks for Name, Number of nights, Room type ____ room, Extra charge for ____. Predicting aloud, the expert thinks: a surname, probably spelled; a small number; a short adjective before “room” (single, double, standard, deluxe); a noun for something paid extra (breakfast, parking, wifi, a pet). Four tight nets set in fifteen seconds — now each answer drops into the net waiting for it while the surrounding chatter slides past unnoticed.

If you finish predicting a set of gaps before the audio starts, do not sit idle. Read ahead into the next set. The pauses are never quite long enough for the slow reader, so the fast predictor banks time and reads into the future.

Ask a struggling candidate to prepare a question and watch what they do: they underline almost every word. An underline on everything is an underline on nothing. Keyword skill is about choosing the few words that will actually help you find the answer, and ignoring the rest.

Not all words are equal. Strong keywords carry the specific meaning of the question (unusual nouns, specific verbs, the topic). Weak keywords are common, low-information words (the, a, some, thing, people) that point nowhere. Unique keywords are unlikely to appear anywhere else in the passage (a proper name, a number, a technical term) and are the most valuable of all. Generic keywords are broad and locate poorly (problem, change, area). Concept keywords carry an idea rather than a word and warn you a paraphrase is coming.

Names, numbers, and dates are almost never paraphrased. Content words almost always are. So your best anchors are the words the exam cannot change: it can turn “cheap” into “won't break the bank,” but it cannot turn the year 1985 into anything except 1985.

Your keyword priority order: 1) unique anchors that cannot change (names, numbers, dates, technical terms) — mark first; 2) strong content words that carry the meaning — mark, but expect them to be paraphrased; 3) concept words that warn a paraphrase is coming — note mentally; 4) weak and generic words — ignore.

Worked example: “In 1996, the company moved its headquarters to ____.” The strongest keyword is 1996, an anchor that cannot be paraphrased. When you hear “in ninety-six,” you know the answer is arriving right now, even if “headquarters” and “moved” are reworded as “relocated its main offices.”
When a question contains a number or a name, that is usually your single best keyword. Circle it and relax about the rest. The exam gave you a word it is not allowed to disguise.

This is the deepest chapter in the module, because paraphrase is the mechanism the whole test runs on. Understand it fully and the exam stops feeling like a trap and starts feeling like a translation you can do.

The question and the audio carry the same meaning in different words. The exam is testing whether you can recognise meaning across changed wording. It is not testing whether you can hear a matching word.

The forms paraphrase takes: (1) synonym — cost becomes price/fee/charge; (2) word-class change — “the decision to close” becomes “they decided to close”; (3) active/passive swap — “the council built the bridge” becomes “the bridge was built by the council”; (4) expression or description — “cheap” becomes “won't break the bank”; (5) indirect wording — the answer is implied rather than stated directly; (6) numerical paraphrase — 50% becomes “half”, doubled becomes “twice as many”; (7) conceptual paraphrase — the whole idea is rebuilt with no shared words at all.

Predict the paraphrase before you listen: this is where prediction and paraphrase meet, and it is the highest-value drill in the module. Take your strong keyword and ask, “If the exam does not use this word, how else might they say it?” Spend two seconds generating alternatives, so your ear is ready for any of them when the paraphrase arrives.

Expert thinking: the question says “The main disadvantage of the site was its ____,” and the audio says “The one real drawback with the location was how far it sat from the station.” A beginner waits to hear the word “disadvantage” and never does, missing the whole sentence. An experienced student catches “drawback” as a match but is a beat late. An expert candidate had already pre-loaded disadvantage = drawback/downside/problem/negative, so “drawback” landed with zero delay and “location” was clearly “site” paraphrased; the answer, distance from the station, was caught cleanly. The expert did not hear better — they expected better.

The words most likely to be paraphrased are the content words in the question. The words least likely to change are names, numbers, and dates. Listen for the meaning of the content words and the sound of the fixed words.

title: 2. Practice · Prediction, Keywords, and Paraphrase Recognition
blocks: Drill 2.1 (Level 1): What shape is the answer?

blocks.title: Drill 2.1 (Level 1): What shape is the answer?
blocks.instructions: For each gap, write the grammatical shape (noun, verb, adjective, number) and the information type.

items.prompt:
1. “The next train departs at ____.”
2. “Please do not ____ the exhibits.”
3. “The workshop is held every ____.” (a day)
4. “Membership costs ____ a month.”
5. “Wear ____ shoes for the walk.”
6. “Leave your bag at the ____ desk.”
items.answer:
1. Number, a time. 2. Verb: touch, photograph, lean on. 3. Noun, a day of the week. 4. Number, a price. 5. Adjective (comfortable, sturdy, waterproof). 6. Noun/role word before “desk” (reception, information, front).
Lesson: every gap tells you its own shape if you read both sides of it.

blocks.title: Drill 2.2 (Level 2): Choose the best keyword
blocks.instructions: For each question, underline the ONE word you would rely on to locate the answer, and say what type it is (unique anchor, strong content, concept).

items.prompt:
1. “How much does the annual pass cost?”
2. “In 2010, the factory switched to solar power.”
3. “The main difficulty with the plan was funding.”
4. “Passengers should report to Professor Nolan.”
5. “The village is famous for its cheese.”
items.answer:
1. cost — strong content, likely paraphrased to price/how much.
2. 2010 — unique anchor, cannot change.
3. funding/difficulty — concept; expect the paraphrase “the hard part,” “money.”
4. Nolan — unique anchor, a name.
5. cheese — strong, fairly unique content word.
Lesson: a name, number, or date in the question usually wins as your keyword.

blocks.title: Drill 2.3 (Level 2): Predict the paraphrase
blocks.instructions: Try it first, then compare with the model answer.

items.prompt: For each keyword, write two or three ways the audio might reword it: buy, dangerous, increase, nearby, important, children.
items.answer:
buy: purchase, pick up, pay for. dangerous: risky, unsafe, hazardous. increase: rise, go up, climb. nearby: close by, within walking distance, a short way off. important: crucial, vital, key, essential. children: kids, youngsters, the young.
Lesson: doing this for two seconds per keyword before the audio is exactly what turns a surprise into an expected event.

blocks.title: Drill 2.4 (Level 3): Match the paraphrase
blocks.instructions: Match each question phrase (1–6) to the audio phrase (A–F) that carries the same meaning.

items.prompt:
Questions: 1. cheap to run 2. difficult to find 3. the decision to expand 4. built in 1990 5. very popular 6. close to the coast
Audio: A. “they chose to grow the business” B. “always packed with visitors” C. “dates back to nineteen ninety” D. “costs very little to keep going” E. “just a short drive from the sea” F. “not easy to track down”
items.answer:
1→D, 2→F, 3→A (note the word-class change: decision→chose, expand→grow), 4→C (the fixed number survives unchanged), 5→B, 6→E.
Lesson: in every pair the meaning is identical while the words are almost entirely different. Train your mind to hear meaning, not words.
